publication_type: Topic-level evidence synthesis combining school bioaerosol field sampling, airborne infection-risk modeling, continuous classroom proxy monitoring, methodological reviews, and official ventilation and infectious-aerosol guidance.
country_and_climate: The evidence spans tropical wet-dry primary schools in Ibadan, Nigeria; temperate and Mediterranean university classrooms in Italy; simulation-based school scenarios in Korea; and international guidance from CDC and ASHRAE. Climate matters because temperature, humidity, rainfall, and seasonal window-opening behavior strongly affect microbial survival, resuspension, ventilation, and the interpretation of proxy signals such as CO2 and particulate matter.
objective_and_research_question: The shared objective is to determine how airborne biological particles in educational buildings can be characterized, when low-cost continuous measurements can serve as useful risk proxies, and which ventilation and air-cleaning interventions most effectively reduce airborne infection risk. For an IoT classroom deployment, the core question is how to combine direct but episodic bioaerosol assessment with continuous proxy sensing and operational decision rules without falsely treating proxy variables as direct pathogen measurements.
study_design: The topic draws on descriptive cross-sectional school studies, seasonal field sampling, respiratory-symptom linkage analyses, multizone simulation using CONTAM plus Wells-Riley, year-round continuous classroom monitoring of CO2 and PM, and review papers on collection and rapid detection technologies for airborne pathogens. Most operational classroom evidence is observational rather than randomized.
educational_context: The directly relevant settings are public primary schools, university classrooms, and connected educational spaces such as corridors. These are high-density environments with prolonged shared-air exposure, repeated daily occupancy cycles, and ventilation systems that range from fully natural ventilation to mixed or HVAC-supported operation.
sample_and_duration: A strong school exposure study is Morakinyo and Ana 2025, which sampled indoor air in 9 randomly selected public primary schools in Ibadan, with occupied and unoccupied classroom sampling performed three times per week for 3 months in the wet season and 3 months in the dry season, alongside a study population of 520 pupils. A complementary continuous proxy-monitoring example is the MIRAI project, which monitored CO2 and PM in 2 Italian university classrooms from March 2022 to May 2023. Simulation evidence adds school-wide airflow and corridor coupling scenarios that cannot be isolated easily in field campaigns alone.
environmental_variables: Bioaerosol and airborne-risk assessment in classrooms should distinguish direct and indirect variables. Direct campaign variables include culturable bacteria and fungi in CFU per cubic meter, size fractions in micrometers, indoor-outdoor differentials, and when available molecular detection of target organisms. Continuous operational variables include indoor CO2 in ppm, PM size-resolved concentration, temperature in degrees Celsius, relative humidity in percent, occupancy pattern, ventilation state, and room connectivity through shared corridors or transfer air paths.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: Outdoor microbial reservoirs, rainfall, dust, wind, and seasonal humidity are major drivers of indoor bioaerosol composition and burden. Interpretation should therefore include outdoor or corridor baseline measurements whenever possible, because naturally ventilated classrooms can import both dilution air and outdoor biological material. Seasonal differences in the Nigerian school study show how wet and dry periods can shift both concentration and respirable fraction.
occupancy_and_activity: Occupancy density, duration of exposure, vocalization, movement, classroom changeover, and the degree of corridor interaction all influence airborne infection risk. Bioaerosol exposure also depends on whether the activity is quiet seated work, active discussion, or a crowded transition period. In infection-risk models, human presence is not only a source term for exhaled aerosols and CO2 but also a determinant of susceptible dose accumulation over time.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: Ventilation and air cleaning are the most actionable control variables for airborne infection risk in classrooms. CDC guidance states that good ventilation helps reduce the number of virus particles in the air, and ASHRAE Standard 241 establishes minimum requirements to reduce exposure to infectious aerosols. The 2025 multizone school simulation adds an important nuance: natural ventilation can reduce pathogen concentration within a classroom but may also increase cross-classroom transmission through corridors if airflow pathways are not managed. In that study, air purifiers and mechanical ventilation reduced within-classroom risk by 42.4% to 91.1% and cross-classroom risk by 78.7% to 80.3%, while some corridor-coupled natural-ventilation scenarios increased cross-classroom infection risk by up to 180%.
spatial_granularity: Bioaerosol risk is strongly location-dependent, so room-level monitoring is the minimum useful scale and corridor coupling can be essential in multi-room buildings. Direct bioaerosol campaigns often need multiple indoor positions, occupied and unoccupied comparisons, and at least one outdoor reference. For continuous proxy monitoring, one well-sited classroom node may be enough for routine operations, but it cannot resolve near-source exposure gradients or corridor-to-room transfer by itself.
sensor_specification: There is no mature low-cost IoT sensor that directly and selectively measures infectious classroom bioaerosols in real time with the ease of a CO2 monitor. Direct measurement still relies on specialized active samplers such as impactors, impingers, filters, cyclones, or electrostatic collectors, followed by culture, microscopy, qPCR, or other laboratory or rapid-detection workflows. For continuous classroom operations, the most practical proxy stack is true CO2 by NDIR plus an optical particle counter or PM sensor, optionally complemented by temperature, relative humidity, and occupancy context. The MIRAI classroom study, for example, used ARANET4 CO2 sensors and optical particle counters covering particle diameters from 350 nm to 40 micrometers.
calibration_and_qaqc: Bioaerosol QA/QC is more demanding than routine IAQ sensing. Active samplers need calibrated flow, sterile media handling, blank controls, documented sampling duration, and careful transport or incubation procedures to avoid sample loss and contamination. For continuous proxy nodes, QA/QC should still include warm-up checks, co-location against better references, timestamp synchronization, and inspection of improbable spikes or flat lines. If culture and molecular methods are combined, the protocol should document whether the target is culturability, total genetic signal, or a rapid-screening biomarker.
acquisition_and_data_quality: Continuous proxy measurements can be collected every 1 to 5 minutes, but direct bioaerosol data usually comes from episodic campaigns lasting tens of minutes to hours, followed by delayed laboratory processing. This means the data architecture must accommodate both high-frequency continuous series and sparse but information-rich direct samples. Missing data, viability loss during collection, blank contamination, culture bias, and changing occupancy during sampling all affect interpretability.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Direct bioaerosol sampling hardware is reusable but operationally maintenance-heavy because pumps, flow calibration, sterile consumables, and laboratory workflows dominate lifecycle effort. Continuous proxy nodes based on CO2 and PM sensing are operationally simpler and can remain in place for long periods, but their value for infection-risk assessment still depends on sustained QA/QC and periodic reinterpretation of local conditions.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: For continuous classroom risk management, recommend true CO2 by NDIR as the primary rebreathed-air proxy, plus PM1 or PM2.5 monitoring, temperature, relative humidity, and occupancy metadata. For direct bioaerosol characterization campaigns, recommend a calibrated active sampler such as an impactor, cyclone, or liquid impinger paired with culture and, when the question requires it, molecular analysis such as qPCR. Real-time pathogen-specific biosensors are promising in the research literature, but they are not yet the default low-cost classroom choice for a TCC-scale deployment.
useful_output_and_units: Useful outputs include CO2 in ppm, PM in micrograms per cubic meter or particle-size distribution, bacterial and fungal burden in CFU per cubic meter, aerodynamic size fractions in micrometers, occupied-period exceedance metrics, indoor-outdoor ratios, and modeled infection risk outputs such as rebreathed fraction, event infection probability, or equivalent removal effectiveness when the modeling assumptions are stated explicitly.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: CO2 and PM are not direct pathogen measurements. CO2 is a rebreathed-air proxy and PM is a broad aerosol burden proxy that includes non-biological particles. Culture, qPCR, and other direct analyses measure collected biological material more directly, but even they do not perfectly reveal real-time infectivity because viability, culturability, and infectious dose are not identical. This distinction is central to defensible classroom monitoring.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: Proxy sensing relies on mature physical principles such as NDIR for CO2 and optical scattering for PM. Direct bioaerosol sampling relies on aerodynamic or electrostatic collection principles such as impaction, impingement, filtration, or cyclone separation, followed by biological identification methods including culture, microscopy, immunologic assays, or nucleic-acid amplification. Reviews from 2024 to 2026 show growing interest in real-time fluorescence, microfluidics, CRISPR-assisted detection, and integrated rapid-detection platforms, but selectivity, viability preservation, and deployment practicality remain limiting factors.
useful_range_and_real_performance: In the Nigerian school study, median total bacterial counts in the wet season exceeded the often-cited indoor guideline of 500 CFU per cubic meter, and fungal counts exceeded the often-cited 50 CFU per cubic meter benchmark, illustrating that school bioaerosol burdens can be substantial even outside an outbreak-specific study. More importantly for deposition risk, 67.5% of bacterial aerosols and 77.8% of fungal aerosols in the wet season were in the respirable 1.1 to 4.7 micrometer size fraction. For continuous operational proxies, the MIRAI study showed that naturally ventilated classrooms had higher and more variable CO2 and PM than HVAC-supported rooms, reinforcing proxy usefulness for screening ventilation-related infection risk even when no direct pathogen data is collected.
operating_regime: A practical classroom program should use continuous proxy sensing year-round and reserve direct bioaerosol campaigns for targeted investigations: recurring symptoms, visible moisture or mold, outbreak periods, filtration intervention studies, or before and after remediation. Event-based sampling during occupied periods and immediately after class changeover is often more informative than arbitrary single-time spot sampling.
interferences_and_confounders: CO2 proxy interpretation is confounded by variable infectivity, occupant activity, masks, outdoor baseline, and ventilation patterns. PM is confounded by dust, chalk, outdoor pollution, and other non-biological sources. Culture methods miss viable but non-culturable organisms, while molecular methods may detect dead organisms and fragments. Well-mixed far-field models can miss near-field exposure and complex multizone flow paths, especially in rooms connected by corridors or transfer air.
affordable_validation_protocol: For a TCC-scale protocol, deploy true CO2 and PM continuously in one or more classrooms, annotate occupancy and ventilation state, and run at least one targeted direct-sampling campaign during representative occupied and unoccupied periods. Use one outdoor or corridor reference, collect blanks, calibrate sampler flow before and after use, and document sampling height and duration. Pair the field results with a simple Wells-Riley or rebreathed-fraction model only after explicitly stating the assumptions and limits of far-field mixing.
validation_metrics: For continuous proxy nodes, report bias, MAE, RMSE, uptime, missing-data fraction, and false-alert frequency. For direct samplers, report flow accuracy, sample duration, blank contamination, colony recovery or qPCR output, and where possible collection or biological efficiency. For infection-risk models, report sensitivity to occupancy, outdoor CO2, quanta assumptions, and ventilation uncertainty rather than only a single point estimate.
installation_and_enclosure: Continuous proxy sensors should sit in the occupied breathing zone, away from direct drafts, windows, doors, and supply jets when the goal is representative room air. Bioaerosol samplers should be installed at documented height with unobstructed inlet flow, using sterile handling and avoiding immediate proximity to walls or localized turbulence unless source tracking is the specific objective. If corridor transfer is suspected, at least one strategically placed shared-space measurement is justified.
hardware_integration: CO2, PM, temperature, and humidity integrate readily with ESP32- or Raspberry Pi-class classroom IoT nodes. Direct bioaerosol collection does not yet integrate cleanly into the same low-cost always-on architecture because pumps, consumables, sterility, and downstream analysis create a separate instrumentation and workflow layer. The practical architecture is therefore hybrid: continuous proxy sensing plus portable or episodic direct-sampling equipment.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] Continuous proxy monitoring can be implemented at classroom-node scale with moderate cost, but direct bioaerosol assessment is substantially more expensive once pumps, calibrated samplers, collection media, consumables, laboratory analysis, and trained handling are included. In practice, the cost gap between a classroom CO2 plus PM proxy node and a defensible direct bioaerosol campaign is large enough that routine school deployment is usually proxy-based, with direct sampling reserved for targeted studies or investigations.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity is high for the value of ventilation and air cleaning in reducing airborne infection risk, moderate to high for CO2 as a useful but imperfect far-field proxy, moderate for PM as a supporting risk indicator, and moderate for school bioaerosol exposure studies involving fungi and bacteria. Evidence maturity remains low for truly real-time, low-cost, pathogen-specific classroom bioaerosol sensing that is selective, validated, and operationally simple.
variable_specific_cautions: Do not equate CO2 with pathogens, and do not equate PM with bioaerosol burden. Culture underestimates total viable burden, while qPCR can overstate viable infectious presence by counting non-viable material. Wells-Riley outputs are model-derived and apply best to far-field, well-mixed assumptions. Corridor coupling, near-field exposure, and occupant activity can make real exposure very different from what a room-average proxy suggests.
system_architecture: A robust architecture is classroom proxy node plus campus network plus time-series database plus alerting and dashboard layer, augmented by a portable campaign toolkit for direct bioaerosol sampling when needed. During normal operation, the system should surface occupancy-normalized CO2 and PM, ventilation events, and building zones that repeatedly show elevated airborne-risk proxies. During targeted investigations, those same timestamps should anchor direct sampling and post-hoc modeling.
connectivity_and_protocols: Wi-Fi with MQTT or HTTPS is typically sufficient for classroom proxy sensing. Because direct bioaerosol campaigns are usually episodic and manually handled, their results can be ingested later as annotated records rather than as a continuous stream. The key interoperability requirement is not exotic protocol support but clean alignment between proxy time series, occupancy logs, ventilation metadata, and any direct microbiological results.
interoperability_and_data_model: The minimum data model should include timestamp, room ID, sensor ID, CO2, PM, temperature, relative humidity, occupancy state if known, QA flags, and ventilation mode. Direct-sampling records should additionally include sampler type, flow rate, collection medium, duration, occupied or unoccupied condition, indoor or outdoor location, and the analysis method used. Without this contextual metadata, bioaerosol comparisons across classrooms and campaigns become weak.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: Proxy monitoring is usually low privacy risk, but outbreak or infection-risk narratives raise institutional sensitivity. Access to room-level risk views should be role-based, and dashboards should avoid stigmatizing individual teachers, students, or programs. If symptom or absenteeism data are linked for research, governance should explicitly separate environmental monitoring from personal health surveillance and comply with the local legal framework.
analytical_methods: Useful analytical methods include descriptive time-series analysis of CO2 and PM, seasonal and occupied-versus-unoccupied comparisons, indoor-outdoor ratio analysis, aerodynamic size-fraction analysis, symptom association, multizone airflow simulation, and Wells-Riley or rebreathed-fraction modeling. The strongest studies combine at least one direct measurement pathway with one operational proxy pathway instead of relying on only one of them.
derived_index_or_model: The most common derived risk tools are rebreathed fraction based on excess CO2, Wells-Riley infection probability, and multizone simulation outputs that account for airflow between connected rooms. These models are valuable because they translate proxy measurements into operational risk logic, but they remain sensitive to assumptions about quanta generation, occupancy, masking, mixing, and pathogen removal processes.
decision_rules_and_standards: Operational rules should follow cleaner-air logic rather than pretend that a single microbial threshold resolves all classrooms. CDC recommends cleaner air and ventilation to reduce airborne virus transmission, and ASHRAE Standard 241 formalizes minimum infectious-aerosol control requirements. For school operations, defensible rules include prioritizing rooms with repeated high occupied-period CO2, addressing moisture or visible fungal contamination immediately, escalating when PM and CO2 remain elevated together under high occupancy, and using direct bioaerosol assessment selectively where complaints, outbreaks, or mold indicators justify it. Because microbial guideline values are not harmonized internationally, they should be treated as contextual reference points rather than universal pass-fail limits.
intervention_and_automation: Core interventions are increased outdoor air, better scheduling of purge ventilation, verified HVAC operation, portable HEPA filtration, cleaner corridor airflow management, and occupancy management during high-risk periods. Automated responses can include alerting staff to open windows or inspect systems, increasing fan or outdoor-air settings where the building permits, and prioritizing portable air cleaners in rooms with persistently poor proxy signals.
environmental_outcomes: Continuous monitoring and targeted intervention improve visibility into stale-air episodes, pollutant buildup during crowded periods, and seasonal shifts in classroom airborne burden. Direct sampling studies also reveal whether the issue is mainly moisture-linked fungal contamination, occupancy-linked bacterial resuspension, or a broader ventilation inadequacy that elevates multiple airborne-risk proxies at once.
health_and_learning_outcomes: The strongest direct school evidence in this set is respiratory morbidity linkage rather than confirmed infection incidence. Morakinyo and Ana 2025 connects seasonal respirable bioaerosol burden with respiratory symptoms among school pupils, while broader guidance and modeling literature support the plausibility that cleaner air reduces airborne infection exposure in schools. For learning settings, the benefit pathway is mainly through healthier air, fewer respiratory complaints, and reduced time spent in poorly ventilated spaces.
objective_subjective_integration: Direct school bioaerosol studies often pair measurements with symptom or morbidity data, while continuous IAQ studies pair sensor values with occupant perception and operational observations. This combination is useful because microbial risk is not always obvious from perception alone, and a classroom that feels acceptable can still exhibit poor ventilation or significant respirable biological burden.
quantitative_results: Morakinyo and Ana 2025 studied 9 public primary schools and 520 pupils, found that wet-season median total bacterial counts exceeded 500 CFU per cubic meter, and reported that 67.5% of bacterial aerosols and 77.8% of fungal aerosols were in the respirable 1.1 to 4.7 micrometer size range. The same study estimated higher absorbed bioaerosol dose in children than adults, including 667 versus 348 CFU per kilogram per day in the wet season. Park et al. 2025 reported that some natural-ventilation scenarios increased cross-classroom infection risk through corridors by up to 180%, while air purifiers and mechanical ventilation reduced within-classroom risk by 42.4% to 91.1% and cross-classroom risk by 78.7% to 80.3%. The MIRAI project found that the naturally ventilated classroom showed higher and more variable CO2 and PM than the HVAC-supported room, supporting proxy use for ventilation-risk screening.
feasibility_and_acceptance: A hybrid monitoring strategy is feasible and credible for educational buildings: continuous low-cost proxies for everyday management, and direct bioaerosol campaigns for focused investigations. Routine acceptance is typically high for CO2 and PM monitoring because the hardware is familiar and non-intrusive. Direct bioaerosol work is less scalable operationally because of cost, laboratory dependence, and interpretive complexity, but it adds value when schools face symptoms, dampness, outbreak concerns, or intervention evaluation needs.
validity_and_limitations: The largest limitation is that direct pathogen presence and infectivity are rarely measured continuously in classrooms. Proxy-to-risk translation depends on assumptions, and microbial sampling results can vary with method, season, and culture or molecular workflow. Many models assume far-field mixing and therefore understate near-source variation, while many field studies are local and may not transfer cleanly across climates, building types, and pathogen contexts.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The literature supports a practical conclusion: classroom airborne-risk management should rely on continuous proxy monitoring for daily operations and targeted direct bioaerosol assessment for higher-resolution investigation. The main gaps are validated low-cost real-time pathogen sensors, harmonized school bioaerosol sampling protocols, better fusion of direct microbiology with classroom IoT streams, and stronger studies linking intervention-driven cleaner air to measurable reductions in infection, symptoms, absenteeism, and inequity across school buildings.
